cover.title: The Army said 'flying disc.' Then took it back.

lines.text: In 1947, the United States Army announced it had captured a flying saucer. The next day... it took it back.
June 1947. A rancher named Mac Brazel finds strange debris scattered across a ranch outside Roswell, New Mexico.
Rubber strips. Tinfoil. Tough paper. Sticks. He brings some of it to the sheriff.
July eighth. The Roswell Army Air Field puts out a press release. They have recovered a flying disc.
The Roswell Daily Record runs it on the front page. R A A F captures flying saucer on ranch in Roswell region.
Within hours, the Army changes its story. It was just a weather balloon.
For thirty years, almost nobody talked about it. Then, in the late seventies, people started coming forward with stories of bodies and a cover up.
In 1994, the Air Force said the debris came from Project Mogul. Secret balloons built to listen for Soviet nuclear tests.
Today, Roswell has a UFO museum, alien street lights, and a UFO festival every summer.
So what crashed? A balloon... or something else? Comment balloon or aliens... and sleep tight, partner.
